en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on Vessantara, Concerning the Question on Inference.
3. The Question on the Greater Strength of the Wholesome and the Unwholesome “Venerable Nāgasena, which is more powerful and stronger: the wholesome or the unwholesome?
“The wholesome, Great King, is more powerful and stronger, not so the unwholesome.”
“Venerable Nāgasena, I do not accept that statement: ‘The wholesome is superior and more powerful, whereas the unwholesome is not so.

For here, venerable Nāgasena, we see those who take life, those who take what is not given, those who engage in sexual misconduct, those who speak falsehoods, village-destroyers, highwaymen, deceivers, and cheats—all of them, by virtue of that much evil, [are seen to prosper].”

They undergo the cutting off of hands, the cutting off of feet, the cutting off of both hands and feet, the cutting off of ears, the cutting off of the nose, the cutting off of both ears and the nose; they are made to drink molten bronze,
have their heads shaved with a conch-shell razor, have their faces carved like Rāhu’s mouth, wear garlands of fire, carry torches in their hands,

are wrapped in straw mats, are clothed in bark, are dressed in animal skins, are impaled on stakes, are branded with copper coins, are scraped with salt and wood, and are forced to turn a heavy millstone.

Being drenched with boiling oil from a straw mat, being devoured by dogs, being impaled on a living stake, and having one’s head cut off with a sword—some who commit evil at night experience the result that very night;
some who commit it at night experience it during the day; some who commit it during the day experience it during the day; and some [who commit it] during the day...
Some experience the result on the very same night after having performed the deed; some experience it after two or three days have passed;
yet all of them experience the ripening of the result in this very life (diṭṭheva dhamme).
But, venerable Nāgasena, is there anyone who [experiences the result] for one, two, three, four, or five [lives]?
“Or having given a gift accompanied by a retinue of ten, or a hundred, or a thousand, or a hundred thousand, will one experience wealth, fame,
or happiness in this very life through that virtue or through the observance of the Uposatha?

“There are, Great King, four kinds of persons who, having given gifts, undertaken virtue, and performed the Uposatha duties, have attained the City of the Thirty-three (Tidasapura) in this very life with that very same physical body.”
“Who were they, venerable sir?
“King Mandhātā, great king, King Nimi, King Sādhīna, and the musician Guttila.

“Venerable Nāgasena, these were separated from you by many thousands of existences; both of them are beyond our perception. If you are able, speak of them while they were still existing, during the time of the Blessed One.”

“Great King, even in the present existence, the slave Puṇṇaka gave food to the Elder Sāriputta and on that very day attained the status of a merchant chief; he is now known as the merchant chief Puṇṇaka.
Queen Gopālamātā, having sold her own hair and with the eight kahāpaṇas she obtained, [gave them] to the Elder Mahākaccāyana...”
Having given almsfood to one who was the eighth [in the order of disciples], she attained the position of chief queen to King Candapajjota on that very day.

The female lay follower Suppiyā, having given a covering for her thigh made from her own flesh to a certain sick bhikkhu, became healed of her wound, with skin restored and free from disease, on the very next day.
Queen Mallikā, having given the Blessed One a lump of last night’s sour gruel, became the chief queen to King Kosala on that very day.
The garland-maker Sumana, having worshipped the Blessed One with eight handfuls of jasmine flowers, attained great prosperity on that very day.

The Brahmin Ekasāṭaka, having worshipped the Blessed One with his upper robe, obtained the position of Sabbatthaka on that very day. All these, O Great King, experienced wealth and fame pertaining to the present life.
“Venerable Nāgasena, after searching and investigating, you have found only six persons.”
“Yes, Great King.
“In that case, venerable Nāgasena, it is the unwholesome alone that is excessive and more powerful, and not so the wholesome.
For one day, venerable Nāgasena, I saw even ten men [suffering] through the ripening of evil karma.”
I see twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, even a hundred or a thousand men being impaled on stakes as the ripening of their evil karma.
Venerable Nāgasena, in the Nanda clan there was a son of a general named Bhaddasāla.
And King Candagutta engaged in battle.
In that battle, venerable Nāgasena, there were eighty headless trunks on both sides of the two armies;
it is said that when one headless trunk fell, another headless trunk would rise up, and all of these were indeed due to evil.
"Through the ripening of that karma, they have fallen into ruin and disaster.
For this reason also, venerable Nāgasena, I say that the unwholesome alone is excessive and more powerful, and not so the wholesome.
Is it heard, venerable Nāgasena, that in this teaching of the Buddha, King Kosala gave an incomparable gift?"
“Yes, Great King, it is heard.
“But, venerable Nāgasena, after giving that peerless gift, did the King of Kosala obtain on account of it any wealth, fame, or happiness pertaining to this present life?
“Certainly not, Great King.”
“If, venerable Nāgasena, even after giving such unsurpassed alms as this, the King of Kosala did not obtain on that account any wealth,
fame, or happiness pertaining to the present life, then, venerable Nāgasena,
it is the unwholesome alone that is excessive and more powerful, and not so the wholesome.”
“Because it is limited, Great King, the unwholesome ripens quickly; because it is vast, the wholesome ripens over a long period of time. This, Great King, should be examined by means of a simile.

Just as, Great King, in the western country there is a kind of grain called *kumudabhaṇḍikā* which, when harvested in the month and brought inside the house, its stalks ripen in five or six months—what then, Great King, is the difference here, what is the distinction?”
“Is it because of the smallness of the lily-bulb and the abundance of the rice?
“Because of the smallness of the lily-bulb, venerable sir, and the abundance of the rice.
Venerable Nāgasena, the rice is fit for a king, a king’s food; the lily-bulb is the food of slaves and laborers.”
“In the same way, Great King, because it is small, the unwholesome ripens quickly; because it is vast, the wholesome ripens after a long time.
“Venerable Nāgasena, that which ripens quickly therein is indeed considered in the world to be superior and more powerful; therefore, the unwholesome is more powerful, and not so the wholesome.”

"Just as, venerable Nāgasena, whatever warrior enters a great, vast battle, seizes the enemy by the armpit, drags him away, and brings him swiftly before his lord—that warrior is called capable and brave in the world.
And whatever physician quickly extracts the arrow and removes the disease—that physician is called skillful.
And whatever accountant calculates very rapidly and presents the result swiftly—that accountant is called skillful."

“Just as that wrestler who quickly lifts his opponent and throws him down onto his back is called a capable and heroic wrestler, even so, venerable Nāgasena, whatever action—whether wholesome or unwholesome—ripens quickly, that is the most preeminent and powerful in the world.
“Both those types of action, Great King, are indeed to be experienced in a future life; however, the unwholesome [is more powerful] because of its blameworthiness.”
In an instant it becomes something to be experienced in this very life. Great King, this rule was established by the kṣatriyas of old:
“Whoever kills a living being is deserving of punishment; whoever takes what is not given... whoever goes to another’s wife...
whoever speaks falsehood... whoever destroys a village... whoever ruins a road... whoever practices fraud... whoever commits deception...”
‘He who does this deserves punishment; he should be flogged, cut, broken, or killed.
Having investigated and deliberated upon that [offense], they punish, kill, cut, break, and strike him.
But, Great King, is there any established rule laid down by anyone such that: ‘Whoever gives a gift or guards their virtue...’?”
“Or if one performs an Uposatha ceremony, should wealth or fame be given to him?”—
“Would they, having deliberated again and again, give wealth or fame, as if for a thief who has committed a crime, by way of execution or imprisonment?”— “Certainly not, Bhante.”
“If, Great King, donors were to give wealth or fame after having carefully selected [the recipient],
then even a wholesome deed might be experienced in the present life. But because, Great King, they do not select a donor with the thought,
‘We shall give wealth or fame,’ therefore the wholesome deed is not experienced in the present life.”
“For this reason, Great King, unwholesome action is to be experienced in the present life, whereas in the future life one experiences a more excessive and stronger feeling.
“Excellent, Bhante Nāgasena! Without a wise person such as yourself, this question could not have been so thoroughly unraveled. Bhante Nāgasena, the mundane has been clarified by the supramundane.
The third question: On the Greater Strength of Wholesome and Unwholesome Actions.
